title: The Sweet Shop Rumour
subtitle: A poisoning rumour empties the market; the easy fix is to cut the internet
coldOpen: 11:20. Six children fall sick after a school lunch.
11:50. A forward blames a sweet shop and says a child died.
By noon, the market lane is empty and the shop is boarded.

briefing.grievance: Parents want to know what made the children sick and whether more sweets are out there. Shop owners want the panic to stop before it ruins them.
knownFacts: Six children are in hospital with food poisoning symptoms; all are stable.
All six ate at the same school event, not at the market.
The named shop supplied nothing to the event.
unverifiedClaims: A forward says one child has died.
A post says the shop uses industrial dye and the city knew.
briefing.responsibility: You coordinate the hospital, food safety and the police. Parents need facts, and a shop needs its name back.
briefing.objective: Find the real source, stop the rumour with facts, and keep the market and the internet open.

rightsMoments.question: A false forward is spreading panic. Can the city order all posts about the incident removed?

options.text: No. It may seek removal of specific false posts and must publish corrections; it cannot silence all discussion.
options.feedback: Correct. Action against speech must be narrow and specific; the remedy for falsehood is mostly more truth.

options.text: Yes. During a public-health scare, any related speech can be suspended.
options.feedback: Scares do not suspend free expression; only specific, lawful and proportionate limits apply.

options.text: Yes, if the platforms agree to it.
options.feedback: A platform’s consent does not make a blanket order lawful.

rightsMoments.principle: Article 19(1)(a) protects expression; the Supreme Court has struck down vague, sweeping speech restrictions. Specific false posts can be addressed; whole topics cannot be banned.
rightsMoments.why: Parents sharing real updates were using the same channels as the rumour; a blanket order would have silenced them too.

simple.question: A fake forward is spreading panic. Can the city delete every post about it?

options.a: No. Only specific false posts, and share the truth widely.
options.b: Yes. In a health scare, all talk about it can be stopped.

feedback.a: Yes! Be specific, and fight lies with facts.
feedback.b: No. A scare does not cancel free speech.
feedback.c: Apps agreeing does not make it fair.

simple.principle: People may speak freely. Only specific false posts can be acted on, and facts are the best answer.
simple.why: Parents sharing real news used the same apps as the rumour. A total ban would silence them too.
